Lessons.Title: Introduction to Liquid Volume
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Grade 3 Unit 6 Lesson7, under CCSS 3.MD.A.2, is a HANDS-ON introduction to LIQUID VOLUME (capacity), not a fixed arithmetic worksheet. The owner-device locally archived teacher lesson.html SHA256 594fd3cea6477a3a8c122389fc81a76607f4642bfdaa4a70a93be67c0aa5f4c1 and preparation.html SHA256 8e80f1ef9cdab2a3be2433a9b31d80c8c3b092dcac9ffdb2c7a1b0132c93055c were read, as were the three 2021 student-facing sections. A standalone original Student Task Statements PDF, original source photographs, blackline/video representations and teacher-only cooldown were not independently retrieved or compared. All first-party diagrams and tasks are independent interpretations; no 100-percent publisher-art parity claimed.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder: The Bowl and the Jar (10 minutes) shows a bowl and jar partly filled with liquid. Students notice and wonder how much each contains or can hold, not simply which appears taller/wider. The teacher defines LIQUID VOLUME as the amount of space liquid takes up. From pictures alone, bowl width and jar height do not determine which capacity is greater. Valid ways to measure: pour into another identical reference container, transfer water from one to other, or use the SAME small unit (e.g., spoon or cup) to count fills. Teacher evaluates open reasoning.

Activity1 Liquid Volume Estimation Exploration (20 minutes) requires a group of FOUR with actual containers distinctly marked A and B plus ONE shared smaller 'unit' container. Teacher chooses A and B with different shapes but similar enough capacity to make estimation meaningful, supplies water, optionally a tray/towel, and asks students to record for EACH vessel three values: TOO LOW, ABOUT RIGHT, TOO HIGH, expressed as a NUMBER OF UNIT-CONTAINER-FULLS. The unknown actual volumes are local physical variables, not source-stated constants. Do not claim an exact A/B capacity or auto-score a particular integer.

Activity1 then has the group repeatedly fill A from the small unit and count, repeat for B with the SAME unit size and fill procedure, then conclude which holds GREATER LIQUID VOLUME and explain the evidence. A larger count using the SAME small unit corresponds to greater capacity; using DIFFERENT unit containers would make the counts incomparable. Teacher can assign filler/recorder roles for A, then swap roles for B. The group may need to decide how to represent residual water if A/B are not exact multiples of unit size; do not force rounded exact units without evidence.

Activity2 Liquid Volume in Liters (15 minutes) introduces the LITER, symbol uppercase L. Teacher brings one known 1-liter container, a supply of water, and a large transparent container that can be marked at increasing fill levels with dry-erase pen. Students FIRST estimate a TOO LOW, ABOUT RIGHT and TOO HIGH number of liters that their actual large container could hold. As a class, they pour water in repeatedly using one full LITER at a time; after each pour, label the new water level with the cumulative number of liters1L,2L,...; bottom corresponds to 0L. Student pairs can alternate as pourer/marker.

The original teacher narrative provides an ILLUSTRATIVE result 'It fit 9 liters, almost10, about9 1/2 liters' for one possible large container. This is teacher SAMPLE RESPONSE, not a source guaranteed measurement of every classroom container. Actual water container size may differ; one teacher may measure fewer/more liters. Only the counted, marked physical experiment establishes the group's result. A prerecorded source instructional video exists as an alternative demonstration, but is not opened or republished; source emphasizes first-hand filling and marking whenever practical.

Activity2 synthesis asks why the marks mimic tick marks on a ruler, why the container BOTTOM represents zero, why successive full 1-liter pours increase total by one, how capital L labels the unit, and which familiar objects can hold similar liquid volumes. MLR5 Co-Craft Questions encourages pupils' own capacity questions; no fixed class response required. The lesson ends with students explaining liquid volume in everyday language, containers with labeled capacity and examples such as beverage or detergent bottles.

The original publisher Cool-down Liquid Volume Reflection is teacher-login gated and is NOT reconstructed as a publisher question. Original photo images include bowl/jar and three containers but pixels were not visually compared or copied. KeyConcepts.Title: Liquid volume / capacity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Liquid volume describes how much space a liquid takes up; vessel capacity is how much liquid container can hold.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use repeated equal volume units to compare.
KeyConcepts.Example: If A takes 8 small identical scoops and B takes 6, A can hold more when scoops are equal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Informal same unit
KeyConcepts.Definition: Counting small reusable unit-container fills provides a comparable measurement when size of that unit remains fixed.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Never compare fill counts measured with different-sized scoops as if they were same unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: One unit spoon used repeatedly for both A and B.

KeyConcepts.Title: Liter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Liter (L) is a standard unit for measuring liquid volume.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Pour a full1-liter unit each time and mark cumulative totals1L,2L,3L...
KeyConcepts.Example: A big vessel that takes five full liter bottles contains5L at fifth marked level.

KeyConcepts.Title: Estimation not actual measurement
KeyConcepts.Definition: Too-low/about-right/too-high estimates bracket plausible volume, but only filling and reading determine actual results.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Judge order low < about-right < high; teacher assesses reasonableness for available vessels.
KeyConcepts.Example: Teacher's9L sample is not a mandatory publisher capacity for every container.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare two real containers using same informal unit
WorkedExamples.Question: How would you decide whether A or B holds more liquid?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count repeated fills from SAME small unit.
Steps: Fill unit once, pour into A and repeat until full; record count.
Empty and measure B using identical unit-fill procedure.
Compare counts and discuss any extra partial fill.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Depends on actual A and B; higher same-unit count means greater capacity
WorkedExamples.Check: Original has no fixed counts for A/B.

WorkedExamples.Title: Pour one liter at a time
WorkedExamples.Question: How should a class label a clear container after its fourth complete liter?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count cumulatively from zero at vessel bottom.
Steps: After fourth pour, mark4L at waterline.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teaching example only, not original class result.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source teacher nine-liter response
WorkedExamples.Question: Does the source mean every class vessel holds9 liters?
WorkedExamples.Method: Distinguish original teacher SAMPLE RESPONSE from student-measured physical quantity.
Steps: The teacher source suggests a container could hold9 complete L plus some extra space.
Other large vessels may have different capacities.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; original example is not a fixed object volume
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher verifies number of full1L pours.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Decide which pictured bowl or jar holds more based solely on height or width.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Different shapes and fill levels can mislead capacity comparisons.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Measure both with same informal unit or transfer and compare.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Give container A, B or big class vessel a predetermined numeric capacity.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Teacher chooses real local containers that can vary.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep numeric answers blank, rely on actual experiment and teacher inspection.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use unequal sized scoops for A and B.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Counts in different units are not directly comparable.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the SAME labeled unit for both.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Label the first poured liter as0L.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Bottom empty vessel is 0L; after first full liter it is1L.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Mark zero at bottom and each successive filled level with cumulative L count.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mistake 9L in sample dialogue for official answer.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source says this is a hypothetical filled teacher container only.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare estimate with actual physical liter counts.

SummaryPoints: Original source warm-up is bowl/jar notice-wonder with liquid volume definition, no fixed visual answer.
Activity1 real containers A/B and one common small unit, THREE estimates per container, actual fill comparison with teacher observation.
Activity2 large class transparent container, three liter estimates, repeatedly pour exactly1L and mark0 at bottom,1L,2L etc; actual count open.
Publisher teacher dialogue around9L/9 1/2L is sample only, not universal answer; unit capital L.
Source pupil PDF, photo pixel parity, video implementation, gated Cool-down, CI tests and Stage D unverified.
